doc.title: Ann Rabson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 21, 2007

title: Piano influences: Mary Lou Williams, boogie woogie, Jimmy Yancey, Leroy Carr
summary: Her father's boogie-woogie albums and a high-school friend's Jimmy Yancey records shaped her piano style.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Okay. Did you have major influences on the piano? People that you —

How many hours do we have here? My first well of course Mary Lou Williams and all those boogie woogie guys that — my dad got me these albums — Pinetop Smith and Albert Ammons, and Meade Lux Lewis and on and on. So that really influenced me. But this guy, this guy who I met when I was a junior in high school played a couple of things for me. He played a man named Jimmy Yancy, who, you know if I had to have only one influence that would be it. And it sounds so simple, what he does. And I truly believe in making things sound simple. Even if they’re not. Because there’s a real beauty in that. And then Leroy Carr, who — I guess he’s really more of an influence on me vocally than as a piano player — but he’s a wonderful player and he wrote wonderful songs, most of which I don’t do. The only one of his I do is “Midnight Hour Blues.”
